topics.title: Overview, Objectives & Key Definitions
topics.concept:
Unit Overview

This unit introduces the integral, the second pillar of calculus. Where the derivative measures instantaneous rate, the integral measures accumulated change — and, geometrically, area under a curve. You will build the integral from Riemann sums, connect it to antiderivatives through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC), and develop core techniques (basic antiderivatives, properties of definite integrals, and u-substitution).

The FTC is the crown jewel: it ties differentiation and integration together as inverse processes. This unit is one of the largest on the exam.

Big picture: Integrating a rate gives the total (accumulated) change; the FTC lets you compute integrals using antiderivatives.

Learning Objectives

  • Approximate area/accumulation with left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums (and the Trapezoidal Rule).
  • Express a definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums.
  • State and apply both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
  • Use properties of definite integrals (additivity, constant multiple, reversing limits).
  • Find antiderivatives / indefinite integrals of basic functions.
  • Evaluate integrals using u-substitution and simple algebraic techniques.
  • Interpret accumulation functions g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt.

Prerequisite Concepts

  • Differentiation (to recognize antiderivatives) and the Chain Rule (for u-substitution).
  • Summation and area of basic regions.
  • Domain awareness (ln|x| for 1/x, etc.).

Key Definitions

  • Antiderivative: F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x). The indefinite integral is ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C.
  • Definite integral: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = the limit of Riemann sums = signed area between f and the x-axis on [a, b].
  • Riemann sum: Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx over subintervals; using left, right, or midpoint sample points.
  • Accumulation function: g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt — total accumulated amount from a to x.

quiz.q: If R(t) is the rate (gallons/min) at which water flows into a tank, what does the integral from 0 to 10 of R(t) dt represent?
options: The total gallons of water added over the first 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: Integrating a rate of change over an interval gives the total accumulated change; here that is the total volume of water added from t = 0 to t = 10.

quiz.q: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, d/dx of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt equals:
quiz.explanation: FTC Part 1 states that if g(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then g'(x) = f(x).

quiz.q: The integral from a to a of f(x) dx equals:
quiz.explanation: An integral over an interval of zero width is 0.

quiz.q: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of x dx.
quiz.explanation: An antiderivative is x^2/2. Evaluate: (2^2)/2 - 0 = 4/2 = 2.

quiz.q: What is the integral of x^3 dx?
quiz.explanation: By the power rule for integration, integral of x^n = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C. For n = 3: x^4/4 + C.

topics.title: Important Theorems & Formulas
topics.concept:
Important Theorems

Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 (FTC-1): If g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt with f continuous, then g'(x) = f(x). With a variable upper limit u(x): d/dx ∫ₐ^{u(x)} f(t) dt = f(u(x))·u'(x) (Chain Rule).

Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 (FTC-2): If F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

Riemann-sum over/under-estimates: for an increasing function, left sums underestimate and right sums overestimate (reverse for decreasing); for a concave-up function, the Trapezoidal Rule overestimates.

Important Formulas

Basic antiderivatives (add + C):

  • ∫ x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) for n ≠ −1; ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x|
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x; ∫ e^(kx) dx = (1/k)e^(kx)
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x
  • ∫ sec² x dx = tan x
  • ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx = arctan x; ∫ 1/√(1 − x²) dx = arcsin x

Properties of definite integrals:

  • ∫ₐᵃ f = 0; ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦᵃ f
  • ∫ₐᵇ f + ∫ᵦᶜ f = ∫ₐᶜ f (additivity)
  • ∫ₐᵇ [k·f] = k∫ₐᵇ f; ∫ₐᵇ (f ± g) = ∫ₐᵇ f ± ∫ₐᵇ g (linearity)
  • Even function: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f; odd function: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 0

quiz.q: A population changes at rate P'(t). The integral from 2 to 5 of P'(t) dt equals:
quiz.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the integral of a rate P'(t) from 2 to 5 gives the net change P(5) - P(2).

quiz.q: A car's velocity is v(t) ft/s. The integral from 0 to 4 of v(t) dt (with v >= 0) represents:
options: the distance traveled in the first 4 seconds
quiz.explanation: Integrating velocity over time gives displacement; when v >= 0, this equals the distance traveled.

quiz.q: Estimate the integral from 0 to 4 of f(x) dx using a right Riemann sum with 2 subintervals, given f(2) = 3 and f(4) = 5.
quiz.explanation: Subinterval width = 2. Right sum uses right endpoints: 2*f(2) + 2*f(4) = 2(3) + 2(5) = 6 + 10 = 16.

quiz.q: Estimate the integral from 0 to 4 of f(x) dx using a left Riemann sum with 2 subintervals, given f(0) = 1 and f(2) = 3.
quiz.explanation: Width = 2. Left sum uses left endpoints: 2*f(0) + 2*f(2) = 2(1) + 2(3) = 2 + 6 = 8.

quiz.q: For a decreasing function f, a right Riemann sum gives what kind of estimate?
quiz.explanation: For a decreasing function, right endpoints give the smallest values on each subinterval, so the right Riemann sum underestimates the integral.

topics.title: Concept Explanations & Solved Examples
topics.concept:
Concept Explanations

Accumulation (6.1, 6.5). Integrating a rate of change gives net change: ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt = f(b) − f(a). In context, "amount at time b" = "starting amount" + "accumulated change": f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt.

Riemann sums (6.2–6.3). Split [a, b] into n pieces of width Δx = (b − a)/n, sample the height at left/right/midpoints, and sum height × width. As n → ∞, the sum → the definite integral. Know which sampling over- or under-estimates based on monotonicity.

The FTC (6.4, 6.7). Part 2 turns area into arithmetic: find an antiderivative, evaluate at the bounds, subtract. Part 1 says differentiating an accumulation function recovers the integrand — the reason differentiation and integration are inverse operations.

u-Substitution (6.9). The reverse of the Chain Rule. Choose u to be an "inside" function whose derivative also appears (up to a constant). Substitute du, integrate in u, then convert back — or, for definite integrals, change the limits to u-values.

Algebraic set-up (6.10–6.11). Before integrating, simplify: split a fraction term-by-term, do long division on improper rational functions, or rewrite x²/(x²+1) = 1 − 1/(x²+1) so standard forms appear (leading to arctan, etc.).

Worked Examples

Example 1 (FTC-2). ∫₁³ x² dx = [x³/3]₁³ = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3.

Example 2 (Right Riemann sum). Estimate ∫₀⁴ f dx with 2 right rectangles, f(2) = 3, f(4) = 5: 2(3) + 2(5) = 16.

Example 3 (u-substitution). ∫ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx: let u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx → ∫ u³ du = u⁴/4 + C = (x² + 1)⁴/4 + C.

Example 4 (FTC-1 with Chain Rule). d/dx ∫₀^{x²} cos t dt = cos(x²)·2x = 2x cos(x²).

Example 5 (Properties). If ∫₀² f = 3 and ∫₂⁵ f = 7, then ∫₀⁵ f = 10; and ∫₀⁵ 5f = 50.

Example 6 (Accumulation in context). A bacteria culture grows at rate 3t (thousands/hour) from 5 thousand: amount after 2 h = 5 + ∫₀² 3t dt = 5 + [1.5t²]₀² = 5 + 6 = 11 thousand.

Example 7 (Absolute value). ∫₀² |x − 1| dx = ∫₀¹(1 − x)dx + ∫₁²(x − 1)dx = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.

quiz.q: The definite integral from a to b of f(x) dx is defined as the limit of:
options: Riemann sums as the number of subintervals approaches infinity
the average of f(a) and f(b)
quiz.explanation: The definite integral is defined as the limit of Riemann sums as the subinterval width approaches 0 (number of subintervals approaches infinity).

quiz.q: If g(x) = integral from 0 to x of (t^2 + 1) dt, what is g'(x)?
quiz.explanation: By FTC Part 1, g'(x) equals the integrand evaluated at x: x^2 + 1.

quiz.q: FTC Part 2 states that the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals:
options: F(b) - F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f
quiz.explanation: FTC Part 2: if F is any antiderivative of f, the definite integral from a to b of f equals F(b) - F(a).

quiz.q: Water flows out of a tank at rate r(t) liters/min. If the tank starts with 100 liters, the amount at time T is:
options: 100 - integral from 0 to T of r(t) dt
quiz.explanation: Starting amount minus total outflow: 100 - (accumulated outflow) = 100 - integral from 0 to T of r(t) dt.

quiz.q: If f(0) = 20 and f'(t) is a known rate, then f(6) equals:
options: 20 + integral from 0 to 6 of f'(t) dt
integral from 0 to 6 of f'(t) dt
quiz.explanation: The accumulation form: f(6) = f(0) + net change = 20 + integral from 0 to 6 of f'(t) dt.

topics.title: Graphical Interpretation, Common Mistakes & Tips
topics.concept:
Graphical Interpretation

  • A definite integral is signed area: area above the axis is positive, below is negative.
  • The accumulation function g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f: g increases where f > 0, decreases where f < 0, has a local max where f changes + → −, and is concave up where f is increasing.
  • Riemann rectangles visibly over/under-shoot depending on where the height is sampled.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting + C on indefinite integrals.
  • Sign error with ∫ sin x dx = −cos x (and the trig antiderivatives generally).
  • Not changing limits (or not converting back) in u-substitution.
  • Treating ∫ (1/x) dx as a power-rule case — it is ln|x|.
  • Mismatching Riemann over/under estimates — depends on increasing/decreasing (and concavity for trapezoids).
  • Dropping the u'(x) factor when differentiating an accumulation function with a non-x upper limit.

AP Exam Tips

  • FTC-2 is your workhorse for exact definite integrals; FTC-1 for derivatives of accumulation functions (watch the Chain Rule).
  • On accumulation free-response, write "amount = initial + ∫ rate" explicitly.
  • For estimates, state whether a sum is an over- or under-estimate and justify with monotonicity/concavity.
  • Recognize u-substitution when a factor is (a constant multiple of) the derivative of another part.
  • Use symmetry (odd/even) to shortcut integrals over symmetric intervals.

Unit Summary

  • The definite integral = limit of Riemann sums = signed area; integrating a rate gives accumulated change.
  • FTC-1: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f = f(x); FTC-2: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a).
  • Master basic antiderivatives, properties (additivity, linearity, symmetry), and u-substitution.
  • Accumulation functions inherit behavior from f via g' = f, g'' = f'.

Next unit: solving differential equations — recovering a function from its rate of change.

quiz.q: For an increasing function f, a left Riemann sum gives what kind of estimate of the definite integral?
quiz.explanation: For an increasing function, left endpoints give the smallest values on each subinterval, so the left Riemann sum underestimates the integral.

quiz.q: Use a midpoint Riemann sum with 2 subintervals to estimate the integral from 0 to 4 of x^2 dx, using midpoints x = 1 and x = 3.
The expression lim (n->infinity) of the sum from i=1 to n of f(x_i) * (delta x) represents:
quiz.explanation: This is the limit of a Riemann sum, which by definition is the definite integral of f over the interval.

quiz.q: The definite integral from 0 to 3 of (2x) dx can be interpreted geometrically as:
options: the area of a triangle with base 3 and height 6, equal to 9
quiz.explanation: The region under y = 2x from 0 to 3 is a triangle with base 3 and height 6, so the area (integral) is (1/2)(3)(6) = 9.

quiz.q: If g(x) = integral from 0 to x^2 of cos(t) dt, what is g'(x)?
quiz.explanation: By FTC with the Chain Rule, g'(x) = cos(x^2) * d/dx(x^2) = cos(x^2) * 2x = 2x cos(x^2).

mock_tests.title: Practice Set A

questions.q: What is the integral of cos(x) dx?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x) + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of a constant k with respect to x?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of a constant k is kx + C.

questions.q: The integral from 0 to 5 of 0 dx equals:
questions.explanation: The integral of the zero function is 0 over any interval.

questions.q: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects:
options: differentiation and integration as inverse processes
questions.explanation: The FTC establishes that differentiation and integration are inverse operations.

questions.q: If the integral from 1 to 4 of f(x) dx = 10, what is the integral from 4 to 1 of f(x) dx?
questions.explanation: Reversing the limits of integration negates the value: -10.

questions.q: If integral from 0 to 2 of f = 3 and integral from 2 to 5 of f = 7, then integral from 0 to 5 of f equals:
questions.explanation: By additivity of integrals over adjacent intervals: 3 + 7 = 10.

questions.q: If integral from 0 to 3 of f(x) dx = 8, what is integral from 0 to 3 of 5 f(x) dx?
questions.explanation: The constant multiple property: integral of 5f = 5 * integral of f = 5 * 8 = 40.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 1 to 3 of x^2 dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative x^3/3. Evaluate: 27/3 - 1/3 = 26/3.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 0 to pi of sin(x) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative -cos(x). Evaluate: -cos(pi) - (-cos(0)) = -(-1) - (-1) = 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 1 to e of (1/x) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative ln|x|. Evaluate: ln(e) - ln(1) = 1 - 0 = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of (3x^2 - 2x) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative x^3 - x^2. Evaluate: (8 - 4) - 0 = 4.

questions.q: What is the integral of (1/x^2) dx?
questions.explanation: Write as x^(-2). Integral = x^(-1)/(-1) + C = -1/x + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of sec^2(x) dx?
questions.explanation: Since d/dx tan(x) = sec^2(x), the antiderivative of sec^2(x) is tan(x) + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of e^(2x) dx?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of e^(kx) is (1/k)e^(kx) + C. For k = 2: (1/2)e^(2x) + C.

questions.q: Using u-substitution, what is the integral of 2x(x^2 + 1)^3 dx?
questions.explanation: Let u = x^2 + 1, du = 2x dx. Integral becomes integral of u^3 du = u^4/4 + C = (x^2 + 1)^4/4 + C.

questions.q: For the integral of cos(3x) dx, the appropriate substitution gives:
questions.explanation: Let u = 3x, du = 3 dx. Integral = (1/3) integral cos(u) du = (1/3)sin(3x) + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of sin(x) cos(x) dx (using u = sin x)?
questions.explanation: Let u = sin x, du = cos x dx. Integral = integral u du = u^2/2 + C = (1/2)sin^2(x) + C.

questions.q: To integrate (x^2 + x)/x, first simplify to:
questions.explanation: Divide each term by x: (x^2 + x)/x = x + 1, which integrates easily to x^2/2 + x + C.

questions.q: To integrate (x^3 + 2x)/x, rewrite the integrand as:
questions.explanation: Divide term by term: (x^3 + 2x)/x = x^2 + 2, which integrates to x^3/3 + 2x + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of 1/(x^2 + 1) dx?
questions.explanation: This is a standard form: the antiderivative of 1/(x^2 + 1) is arctan(x) + C.

mock_tests.title: Practice Set B

questions.q: Which technique is most appropriate for the integral of x cos(x^2) dx?
questions.explanation: Because the derivative of x^2 (namely 2x) appears (up to a constant), u = x^2 makes this a straightforward substitution.

questions.q: The integral of a sum of functions equals:
questions.explanation: Integration is linear: the integral of (f + g) equals the integral of f plus the integral of g.

questions.q: Let g(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt. If f(x) > 0 on an interval, then g is:
questions.explanation: Since g'(x) = f(x) > 0, the accumulation function g is increasing wherever f is positive.

questions.q: A table gives f(0) = 2, f(2) = 5, f(4) = 6. Estimate the integral from 0 to 4 of f dx with a right Riemann sum (2 subintervals).
questions.explanation: Width 2, right endpoints f(2) and f(4): 2(5) + 2(6) = 10 + 12 = 22.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from -1 to 1 of x^3 dx.
questions.explanation: x^3 is an odd function integrated over a symmetric interval [-1, 1], so the integral is 0. (Check: [x^4/4] from -1 to 1 = 1/4 - 1/4 = 0.)

questions.q: What is the integral of (4x^3 - 6x + 5) dx?
questions.explanation: Integrate term by term: 4x^4/4 - 6x^2/2 + 5x = x^4 - 3x^2 + 5x + C.

questions.q: If F(x) = integral from 2 to x of (t^3) dt, then F'(2) equals:
If integral from 1 to 5 of f = 12 and integral from 1 to 3 of f = 4, then integral from 3 to 5 of f equals:
questions.explanation: By additivity: integral 1 to 5 = integral 1 to 3 + integral 3 to 5, so 12 = 4 + (integral 3 to 5), giving 8.

questions.q: What is the integral of e^(x^2) * 2x dx?
questions.explanation: Let u = x^2, du = 2x dx. Integral = integral e^u du = e^u + C = e^(x^2) + C.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 1 to 2 of (1/x^2) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative -1/x. Evaluate: -1/2 - (-1/1) = -1/2 + 1 = 1/2.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative x^2 + x. Evaluate: (9 + 3) - 0 = 12.

questions.q: What is the integral of 3/(x^2 + 1) dx?
questions.explanation: The constant factors out: 3 * integral 1/(x^2 + 1) dx = 3 arctan(x) + C.

questions.q: If the velocity of a particle is v(t) = 3t^2, the displacement from t = 0 to t = 2 is:
questions.explanation: Displacement = integral from 0 to 2 of 3t^2 dt = [t^3] from 0 to 2 = 8.

questions.q: Increasing the number of subintervals in a Riemann sum generally:
options: improves the accuracy of the approximation
questions.explanation: As the number of subintervals increases (width decreases), the Riemann sum approaches the exact value of the definite integral.

questions.q: What is the integral of (ln x)/x dx?
questions.explanation: Let u = ln x, du = (1/x) dx. Integral = integral u du = u^2/2 + C = (1/2)(ln x)^2 + C.

questions.q: What is the integral of sin(x) dx?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of sin(x) is -cos(x) + C.

questions.q: Let g(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt. If f is negative on (a, b), then on that interval g is:
questions.explanation: g'(x) = f(x) < 0 there, so g is decreasing wherever f is negative.

questions.q: The width of each subinterval when [a, b] is divided into n equal parts is:
questions.explanation: Dividing an interval of length (b - a) into n equal subintervals gives width delta x = (b - a)/n.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral from 1 to 4 of (2/sqrt(x)) dx.
questions.explanation: 2/sqrt(x) = 2x^(-1/2). Antiderivative 4x^(1/2). Evaluate: 4(2) - 4(1) = 8 - 4 = 4.

questions.q: If F is an antiderivative of f and F(1) = 3, F(4) = 11, then integral from 1 to 4 of f(x) dx equals:
questions.explanation: By FTC Part 2: integral = F(4) - F(1) = 11 - 3 = 8.
